This update lowers costs by 30% and provides better consistency for your professional projects. You can start using these capabilities today across the Gemini API, Google Vids, and Gemini for business to produce high-quality video content at scale.

 Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

 We are launching Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash with support for fifteen-second videos and improved reference adherence.

 You can now edit clips through multi-turn conversations, which allows for faster adjustments without starting over.

 We reduced the price by 30% to help you produce high-quality video content at a lower cost.

 This model is generally available on the Gemini API and Google Cloud for your production needs.

 Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental.

 Explore other styles:

 General summary

 Bullet points

 Today, we’re rolling out Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, and making it generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business . Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash introduces native 15-second video creation, multi-turn conversational editing capabilities, and enhanced reference following. We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.
 Here’s an overview of what’s new:
 Fast and cost-effective at scale
 Beyond the lower price, the workflow keeps costs down: you can draft fast at 360p or 720p, fix a detail with a follow-up edit instead of re-generating the entire clip, and then upscale your best creations to 1080p or 4K.
 Longer clips up to 15 seconds
 You can now generate and edit videos natively up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1. You can also specify duration in one-second increments from 3 to 15 seconds, giving you room to tell complete stories, create product explainers, or produce full social ad spots in a single generation.
 Better reference adherence
 You can guide generation combining character, product, or style images, short motion clips (up to three seconds), and audio cues — and Omni 1.2 Flash holds onto those details from start to finish. Faces, garments, packaging typography, and brand colors stay consistent across camera angles, making it easy to turn existing product photography or character sheets into virtual try-on clips, catalog spins, and branded video ads.

 Combining one model photo with front-and-back product shots of three outfits, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates a 15-second virtual try-on sequence across 360-degree turns and match cuts while keeping the model’s identity and each garment’s cut, drape, and back details consistent.

 More consistent results
 You can maintain stronger character, object, and scene consistency from the first to the last frame, with less visual drift or morphing across motion and camera transitions. Whether you’re interpolating between a first and last keyframe, or extending a clip to build a longer sequence, products, characters, props, and environments stay consistent from shot to shot.

 Given the same static studio lighting exhibition poster and five-layer animation prompt, Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash does not match the reference image as closely as 1.2 does. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash builds the poster sequentially layer by layer on the dusty-pink cyclorama rising the hexagonal plinth, assembling the ribbed glass, warm filament, faceted crystal, and coiled-cord letterforms for HALO, GLOW, and LUMEN, and locking every material, shadow, and typographic detail consistently through the final frame.

 Easier editing in conversation
 You can refine the same clip turn by turn — such as swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio — instead of starting over from scratch. Multi-turn conversational editing works across full 15-second clips, making it easy to produce ad variants for different audiences and placements without re-briefing or re-generating.

 Starting from one generated clip, multi-turn conversational prompts swap the background turn by turn — from a striped pavilion tent to an oak forest, a stable with a white horse, a market fair, and a stone castle — while keeping both characters’ performances, armor reflections, and camera framing intact.

 More natural speech
 You can generate scenes with more fluid, natural-sounding dialogue, clearer lip-sync, and distinct multi-speaker conditioning. This will show up whether you’re directing multi-character dialogue in Flow , creating video explainers in Gemini for business , or creating polished, pro videos with avatars, music and narration in Google Vids .

 Conditioned on one conservatory scene image alongside four character, mouth, and one-second voice references, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash routes each sampled voice to the right character with expressive lip-sync and natural comedic timing across a 15-second animated scene.

 More controllable, cinematic look
 You can direct complex, continuous camera movements like sweeping FPV flythroughs to dramatic zoom-outs and orbits with significantly fewer unwanted jump cuts, steadier scale, and a more polished, cinematic look.

 Guided by two architectural reference photos, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash directs one continuous FPV drone flight across the piazza, through the bronze doors, and up through the Pantheon’s coffered dome to the oculus with zero jump cuts.

 Longer clips with smoother motion and tighter consistency
 Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generates clips up to 15 seconds long that hold references together better than before. You can scroll through to see characters, text, and camera moves stay consistent across longer shots, multiple turns and transitions with no cuts.

 15 second long clips: Turns one style frame into a 4-shot, 15-second macro science explainer with accurately spelled, motion-tracked callouts. 

 Multi-turn motion transfer: Generates a rippling octopus in Turn 1, then replaces it in Turn 2 with a dancer whose gown mirrors the exact fluid motion. 

 First-to-last frame consistency (1.1 vs. 1.2): Connects an exterior start frame and interior end frame in one continuous camera push in 1.2 Flash. You can see subtle differences like the cats on the roof, the soup ladle turning into chopsticks, and some other minor changes. 

 Unbroken crash zoom-out: Pulls continuously from a tight shoreline close-up to an aerial island vista in one 10-second shot with natural scale and zero cuts. 

 Real-world results, from creatives to global brands

 Businesses, startups, and creatives are already using Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash in their workflows. And for the first time, Gemini Omni is now generally available, backed by Google Cloud’s enterprise-grade infrastructure and security. Provisioned Throughput is available, and outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.

 Get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash
 While development is ongoing to further improve things like fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics, Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is ideal for businesses, developers, and creators producing videos at scale. You can get started with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash today as it rolls out across Google’s products and developer platforms:
 For developers using the Gemini API: Prototype in Google AI Studio , explore interactive starter apps, and check out the developer documentation and pricing .
 For businesses: Try it in the Google Cloud console , and build enterprise solutions with the API .
 For everyone using Google apps: Direct scenes and multi-turn edits in Flow , generate 15-second clips at no additional cost in Google Vids with a Google account or Google Workspace subscription, create 15-second videos in the Gemini app (rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers), and scale video campaigns in Google Ads .

items.title: Detecting signs of hypertension using wearable sensors
items.content:
Detecting signs of hypertension using wearable sensors

 November 5, 2026
 Paolo Di Achille, Staff Research Scientist, and Ming-Zher Poh, Senior Staff Research Scientist, Google Research

 We present a new AI system that leverages standard consumer smartwatch sensors to passively detect signs of high blood pressure.

 Quick links

 Nature paper 

 Share 

 Copy link 

 ×

 Hypertension (i.e., high blood pressure), often called the "silent killer”, affects over one billion people globally, yet more than half of adults with the condition are unaware they have it . Because it rarely presents with obvious symptoms, high blood pressure (BP) is typically discovered only through incidental screening. This gap in awareness is particularly severe among younger adults aged 18 to 44 , where missing diagnoses can delay life-saving early interventions and significantly increase the long-term risk of adverse cardiovascular events like stroke or heart failure.
 Office BP measurement serves as the primary initial screening gateway for detecting hypertension. In recent years, cuffless wearable devices have emerged as a potential tool to complement episodic office care. However, existing commercial solutions usually require regular calibration using a traditional arm cuff. This means they only track relative changes from a baseline cuff reading rather than identifying absolute hypertensive states, limiting their utility as independent screening tools.
 In a new study published in Nature , we present a multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) system capable of passively detecting signs of hypertension using a consumer smartwatch, without requiring any cuff calibration. Dubbed AI-PPG-ACC-HTN , we validated this system against the clinical gold standard of 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), and it achieves accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuff-based diagnostic workflows for both initial and confirmatory screening. These research findings helped inform the blood pressure trends Health Guardian feature in the Google Health app.

 How it works
 Instead of attempting to estimate exact, point-in-time systolic and diastolic blood pressure values, which are highly susceptible to transient environmental noise, our system reframes the problem. It focuses on identifying an individual’s underlying, persistent hypertensive state by aggregating passive physiological signatures over multiple days.
 The system leverages data from two sensors already active on modern smartwatches:
 Photoplethysmography (PPG): An optical sensor that tracks changes in blood volume at the wrist by measuring reflected light that captures pulse wave contours.
 Accelerometry (ACC): A motion sensor that identifies periods of stillness and captures the ballistocardiogram (BCG) , the subtle physical vibrations of the wrist caused by the mechanical ejection of blood from the heart into the aorta.

 The AI system uses photoplethysmography (PPG) and accelerometer (ACC) signals recorded using a consumer smartwatch to create waveform embeddings. The waveform embeddings are aggregated over time (days) into a person-level embedding, which, along with a user’s height, are used to predict their blood pressure status. 

 To build this system, we used a two-stage machine learning approach:

 Stage 1: Self-supervised pre-training (the waveform encoder)
 We trained a 1-D deep convolutional neural network using self-supervised contrastive learning. By analyzing a large, unlabeled dataset of 492,347 hours of sensor data from 2,109 consenting participants, the model learned to map overlapping 15-second PPG and ACC waveforms from the same individual close together in a latent space. This allowed the model to discover complex, physiologically rich features of vascular and mechanical cardiac function without requiring manual feature engineering or medical labels.

 Stage 2. Person-level aggregation & classification
 For each user, these 15-second feature blocks (embeddings) are mean-aggregated across multiple days of wear to wash out ephemeral noise like sudden movements or temperature changes. Finally, the individual's aggregated embedding is combined with their height (which serves as a reliable proxy for arterial path length) and fed into a regularized logistic regression classifier to calculate a continuous hypertension probability score.

 Rigorous validation against the clinical gold standard
 To evaluate our system, we conducted a prospective, multi-center clinical study across five US sites involving 196 consenting diverse participants who were free from known cardiovascular disease and not taking blood pressure medications.
 Importantly, we benchmarked the smartwatch's performance against 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM), the clinical gold standard for hypertension diagnosis. We evaluated the smartwatch system across two clinical use case scenarios: initial screening and confirmatory testing.

 Scenario 1: Initial screening
 The smartwatch achieved a moderate sensitivity of 65.8% and a high specificity of 90.0%, resulting in a high positive predictive value (PPV) of 80.6%. In comparison, initial office-based screenings showed a sensitivity of 55.3% and a moderate PPV of 77.8% when benchmarked against the gold standard.

 Scenario 2: Confirmatory testing
 For individuals who initially screen positive for high blood pressure in a clinic, current guidelines recommend confirmatory out-of-office tracking. We looked at the subset of participants (N=48) who had elevated initial office BP to see how well the smartwatch could confirm sustained hypertension.
 Our multimodal system achieved a moderate sensitivity of 78.4%, a high specificity of 90.9% and a high PPV of 96.7%. In comparison, the performance of return office BP measurements showed lower point estimates of sensitivity (67.6%), specificity (63.6%), and PPV (86.2%). Furthermore, the smartwatch approach proved competitive with multi-day home monitoring, which yielded a sensitivity of 89.2%, specificity of 81.8%, and a PPV of 94.3%.

 Taken together, the results show that our system can detect hypertension with accuracy levels comparable to traditional cuffed BP devices in the existing clinical framework.

 Model interpretability
 To gain an understanding of what the AI model may be paying attention to, we visualized the average pulse waveforms from users with the highest and lowest predicted probabilities of hypertension.
 We observed the following visual differences:
 Reduced pulse width: Waveforms linked to a higher risk of hypertension exhibited a slightly narrower pulse width (figure below, top left panel), indicating a smaller change in blood volume, and may suggest stiffer arteries that are less able to expand.
 Pulse wave reflection: Higher AI risk scores correlated with a slower systolic upstroke (the initial surge of blood) (figure below, highlighted yellow circle in middle panel) and a lower d/a ratio (figure below, highlighted yellow circle in right panel). This specific metric compares the initial forward-traveling pulse wave to the reflected wave bouncing back from the body's vascular network.
 Mechanical heart vibrations: The smartwatch accelerometer successfully captured the ballistocardiogram (BCG) signal. In users with higher predicted hypertension, we observed distinct physical modulations in these micro-vibrations, specifically deeper "K waves" and wider "IJK complexes" (figure below, highlighted yellow circle in bottom left panel).

 Mean pulse waveforms (top left panel), corresponding accelerometer waveforms showing the ballistocardiogram (BCG, bottom left panel), first (middle panel) and second derivatives (right panel) of pulse waveforms from four of the most extreme quintiles of AI-PPG-ACC-HTN scores. Key fiducial points are indicated including the pulse onset (ons), peak (sys), dicrotic notch (dic), diastolic peak (dia) in the PPG waveform, H, I, J, K, L, M, N waves in the BCG waveform, and a, b, c, d, e waves in the second derivative of the PPG waveform.

 Outlook
 Smartwatch-based hypertension screening is not intended to replace standard clinical arm cuffs or provide a definitive standalone medical diagnosis. Instead, this research points to the potential for a highly scalable, passive tool for opportunistic screening . This work represents early feasibility research and methodologies described here are purely exploratory and are not indicative of any existing or upcoming commercial product feature or device capability. By gently prompting at-risk individuals to step into a clinic for formal assessment, this technology holds the potential to significantly close the global awareness gap and catch hypertension before it causes permanent cardiovascular damage.

 Acknowledgements
 This research was a collaborative effort between Google Research, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, and Harvard Medical School. We thank our paper co-authors Lawrence Cai, Jiang Wu, Mingwu Gao, Bhavna Daryani, Jonathan Wang, Utkarsh Khanna, Ho Ko, Anupam Pathak, Mark Malhotra, Shwetak Patel, Jacqueline B. Shreibati, Stephen P. Juraschek, Pramod Rudrapatna, and Matthew Thompson. We thank key contributors including: Jennifer Block, Anu Gabbita, Sushalini Sunku, Keerthana Natarajan, Alexandros Pantelopoulos, Tuan Phan, Tracy Giest, and Florence Thng.

items.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
items.summary:
AI agents can generate code at a scale that’s hard for humans to review line-by-line. PDD Kit helps ensure the code is doing what the developer intended by creating formal specifications and testing against them. It converts developer intent into a Verus specification, proves AI-generated code meets it for every input, and uses tests where proofs aren't practical. Developers review intent, not every line. 

 The post Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit appeared first on Microsoft Research .
items.content:
At a glance

 Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here.

 Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. 

 PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach.

 We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. 

 The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it.

 Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. 

 This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up.

 So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in.

 PODCAST SERIES 

 The AI Revolution in Medicine, Revisited

 Join Microsoft’s Peter Lee on a journey to discover how AI is impacting healthcare and what it means for the future of medicine.

 Listen now 

 Opens in a new tab 

 Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical.

 Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it.

 How PDD Kit works

 PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document.

 The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact , a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. 

 Figure 1. Proof-Driven Development with PDD Kit. Team members settle intent. Verus and the test suite hold the code to it. 

 Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: 

 Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab) , a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science.

 Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof.

 The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) : the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. 

 The capstone: a full-stack web app

 To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab) . The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust.

 For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: 

 Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: 

 You only get a token with the right password. 

 Only admin accounts get admin tokens. 

 We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job.

 Step 1: Questions before code

 PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. 

 Figure 2. The first decision card. “Only with the right password” on its own is also met by a login that refuses everyone. Proving both ways rules that out. 

 The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways.

 Step 2: A human readable intent map

 As the conversation goes on, PDD Kit keeps a rough work section at the top of the plan current, so a user can keep track of important concepts without having to scroll back through a long chat to find what was agreed. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3).

 Figure 3. PDD Kit’s mental model for login. The field you send picks the window, the window picks the table and with it the role, and nothing prints until the password matches. 

 Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent.

 Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end. 

 The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token.

items.title: The Wizard of Open Weights: Chris Alexiuk Makes AI Easy With Open Models
items.summary: Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it. “We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers.  […]
items.content:
Chris Alexiuk has a simple rule about open source AI: If you believe in it, be loud about it. 

 “We should be shouting about this technology from the rooftops,” said Alexiuk, a Toronto-based senior product research engineer in deep learning at NVIDIA who specializes in making open large language models (LLMs) practical for working developers.  

 Alexiuk’s preferred “rooftop” is YouTube , where he’s built a following teaching curious thousands how to build, fine-tune, evaluate and ship production LLM applications and agents.  

 “I think the people who will most help us understand how to build and apply AI likely haven’t even heard of it yet,” he said. “Trying to get knowledge and information out to as many people as humanly possible is what continues to drive me.” 

 Bringing NVIDIA Nemotron to Developers Everywhere 

 Having spent years teaching developers to build with open models, Alexiuk has concluded that transparency isn’t a feature of good AI; it’s the precondition for it. 

 “Fully open source AI is necessary for the democratization of intelligence,” he said. “You should have access to the weights, the data that went into it, the training recipes, everything.” 

 That’s why, on his LinkedIn profile, Alexiuk styles himself “No. 1 Nemotron Fan,” referring to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of open source, multimodal models built for long-running, self-evolving and specialized AI agents. 

 “I think Nemotron is the most important project that exists,” said Alexiuk, who also uses the pseudonym “Joe Nemotron” across social media. “I’m a firm believer that openness is a very important thing to undertake, so I’m going to be the No. 1 fan of whoever is doing that the best. And that is Nemotron.” 

 https://blogs.nvidia.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ChrisAlexiuk_captions_9MB.mp4 

 It’s this matter-of-fact directness and affable approachability that makes Alexiuk’s teaching style so appealing. On the social media platform X, he goes by the handle “llm_wizard.” His avatar: a laughing cartoon caricature sporting a slouchy sorcerer’s hat and brandishing a magic wand.  

 It’s no surprise, then, that Alexiuk likens Nemotron to a magical library — its users fellow wizards in search of knowledge that can move mountains. 

 “You’re a wizard in search of prepared spells, and Nemotron has a spell for everything,” he said. “Just choose the one you need.” 

 In non-wizard terms? 

 “There’s a category of model that’s going to be close to the kind of work you want to accomplish,” Alexiuk said, explaining that Nemotron supports that whole ecosystem of AI users: from individual developers using a model like Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for repetitive, high-frequency execution work to a company deploying Nemotron Ultra for long-running autonomous agents, deep research and enterprise tasks. 

 NVIDIAN Chris Alexiuk (left) engages with developers during the Build-a-Claw event at GTC Berlin. 
 “I think that openness helps more people understand AI and hopefully leads to more people doing really ingenious things with these tools at the limit,” Alexiuk said. “If a tool is amplifying skill, it’s amplifying human expression.” 

 From Birding to Model-Building 

 Alexiuk first became fascinated with machine learning in a computational physics class at Trent University in Ontario, Canada. 

 “After that, I learned about TensorFlow and that you could build image classifiers that ran on your GPU,” he recalled. As an initial one-off project, Alexiuk built a classifier that would alert him whenever his friend’s distinctive pet bird, a Yellow-Faced Gray Budgerigar, appeared in frame on his webcam during shared video game sessions. 

 “Because we were playing video games, I wasn’t focused on my friend’s webcam, but I didn’t want to miss seeing the bird when it appeared,” Alexiuk said. “And then my whole life changed, because in that instance I realized it’s crazy what you could do with technology.” 

 Since then, he’s been embedding himself in the open source AI community.  

 “To imagine within the span of a few years going from freaking out because I could know my friend’s bird was in the camera frame to being able to make any website in a matter of minutes with a model that’s running on my laptop — I cannot wait to see what’s next,” Alexiuk said. “It’s never been more accessible to get into and learn about AI.” 

 And if another LLM wizard arises to challenge him for the title of No. 1 Nemotron Fan? 

 “It would be the greatest day of my life to be surpassed by an even bigger fan of Nemotron, who had heard about Nemotron through the work I was doing,” Alexiuk said. “That would be a capstone to my career that I can only dream of.” 

 Hear more from Alexiuk by following the NVIDIA Nemotron Labs Livestreams series on YouTube.

items.title: More Performance From Every Byte: How Full-Stack Codesign Solves AI’s Memory Challenge
items.summary: Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack.  […]
items.content:
Larger models, longer contexts and agentic applications are increasing GPU memory pressure while supply tightens and prices rise — a trend expected to continue through the near term. 

 NVIDIA works closely with memory partners to rapidly adopt the latest memory technologies. NVIDIA was first to adopt HBM3e and HBM4 technologies into an accelerated computing stack.  

 But the approach isn’t to simply pack more memory onto the GPU. It’s full-stack codesign. NVIDIA intentionally designs GPUs, CPUs, networking, storage and software together to get more useful work out of memory at every layer of the AI factory. 

 That matters because an AI factory runs on a memory and storage hierarchy. GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the fastest, most expensive and most contested tier — with model weights and KV cache competing for limited capacity. Below it sit CPU memory, local SSDs and shared storage, each trading speed for more capacity at a lower cost per bit.  

 How much useful work a byte does depends on how well the whole hierarchy is used: shrinking what must be stored, placing it on the right tier and bringing it back to the GPU before it’s needed.  

 Byte for byte, NVIDIA makes the most efficient use of memory at every layer — and the results show it. From NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra to the Vera Rubin platform, HBM capacity per GPU rose roughly 3%, while agentic throughput per dollar rose by up to 30x on SemiAnalysis AgentX. 

 Agentic Inference Is Putting More Pressure on HBM 

 Frontier models now have trillions of parameters — the values that hold what an AI model learned in training. 

 KV cache, which holds the context the model needs to understand each active request without reprocessing the same information, is also expanding. Agentic trajectories carry prior context across repeated model and tool calls, in some cases processing up to 3 million tokens, so each request’s working memory grows over time.  

 Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) adds relevant enterprise information to prompts, creating even more context to process and retain.  

 During inference, HBM primarily holds both model parameters and KV cache. The result: greater pressure on HBM.  

 Why AI Factories Need a Memory Hierarchy  

 Adding more HBM capacity per GPU is the obvious response to that pressure, but capacity delivers only what bandwidth can move.  

 Think of HBM as a warehouse and memory bandwidth as its loading docks. A larger warehouse holds more inventory, but the docks set how much can move in and out at a time. Once the docks are at capacity, moving more inventory takes longer and slows response times. If delays exceed the required service level, the added space can’t be used effectively, even as it adds cost and draws power.  

 That’s also why no operation keeps all its inventory in the closest, fastest space. What’s in motion stays near the line. What’s waiting moves to a larger, cheaper space nearby and returns before it’s needed.  

 An AI factory faces the same limit.  

 More HBM can hold more KV cache and support more concurrent users. Every added user shares the same compute and memory bandwidth. But when each user expects fast responses, eventually memory bandwidth is unable to supply data as fast as compute can use it: a limit engineers call the memory wall.  

 Past that point, extra HBM capacity can’t be put to work, yet it still adds costs and draws power. The data still needs a place to live, but not all of it needs the fastest, most expensive tier. This is why an AI factory manages data across a memory and storage hierarchy.  

 Maximizing the Value of Every Byte With Full-Stack Codesign 

 NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign makes every byte of HBM count by relieving pressure from model weights, KV cache and RAG data. It does this with techniques that each target a different source of inefficiency:  

 Shrink model weights and distribute them across the NVL72 domain. 

 The NVFP4 format reduces the space required for weights compared to FP8, the lowest precision possible on the NVIDIA Hopper platform. Recent models, including FLUX.2 [klein] from Black Forest Labs , Inkling from Thinking Machines Lab, Beam 1.0 from Reflection , Meta Muse Spark from Meta , Step 5 Preview from StepFun and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL have been released with NVFP4 checkpoints, demonstrating growing model-builder adoption of 4-bit precision for faster, more memory-efficient inference.  

 Within an NVL72 system, model weights can be distributed across up to 72 GPUs , so each GPU holds a smaller share of the model — leaving more HBM for KV cache and concurrent users.  

 Shrink KV-cache and offload inactive context to lower-cost storage tiers. 

 Applying NVFP4 to the KV cache reduces its footprint compared with FP8, so more context can stay resident in HBM. 

 NVIDIA Vera CPU helps in two ways. Faster tool execution shortens the time KV cache sits inactive during tool calls, and its large LPDDR memory, connected to NVIDIA Rubin GPUs over NVIDIA NVLink-C2C interconnect, gives paused context a nearby place to wait and return quickly.  

 When context isn’t actively in use, NVIDIA Dynamo inference software moves it to NVIDIA CMX context memory storage — a tier built for capacity at far lower cost per bit than HBM — and returns it before reuse. Unlike local SSDs, CMX is shared across servers, and unlike enterprise storage, it skips the overhead of long-term data protection that short-lived context doesn’t need. NVIDIA CMX context memory storage partners include Cloudian , DDN , Dell Technologies , Everpure (previously Pure Storage), HPE , IBM , NetApp , VAST and WEKA .  

 Dynamo’s KV Cache Reuse ties the tiers together, managing KV cache as one system-wide resource across GPU memory, CPU memory and storage, so context computed once can be reused across the system.  

 Compact RAG embeddings and keeping the index outside HBM. 

 RAG turns enterprise documents into embeddings — numerical representations that let a system search by meaning rather than keyword — organized into a searchable index. NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever models produce smaller embeddings with higher retrieval accuracy, while the NVIDIA cuVS library enables that index to be built and served across CPU and storage. The knowledge base never occupies HBM, and only the passages the model needs enter context.  

 The result is less HBM used for model weights, less HBM tied up by idle context and more of it available to serve concurrent users.  

 More Useful Output per Dollar With Each Generation 

 Across successive NVIDIA platform generations, tokens per second per dollar has risen far faster than HBM capacity.  

 On the SemiAnalysis AgentX DeepSeek V4 Pro workload, NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 delivers up to 10x higher throughput per dollar than NVIDIA H200 platform at 100 tokens per second per user, with HBM capacity per GPU roughly doubling. At 125 tokens per second per user, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivers up to 30x higher throughput per dollar than GB300 NVL72, with HBM capacity per GPU up about 3%.  

 For AI factory operators, the metric that matters is how many useful tokens the factory can deliver within its power budget while meeting user response-time needs. More tokens per second per watt means more work and revenue from the same power, and a lower cost for every token. NVIDIA’s full-stack codesign lowers token costs by increasing the useful work every byte of memory delivers.  

 Learn more in the video explainer and technical deep dive on how NVIDIA full-stack codesign reduces inference memory pressure.

items.content:
Data Center / Cloud 

 Configure, Certify, and Operate Kubernetes GPU Clusters with NVIDIA DSX OS

 Nov 05, 2026

 By Sowmyan Soman and Kai Wombacher 

 Like

 Discuss (0)

 L 

 T 

 F 

 R 

 E 

 AI-Generated Summary

 NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform provides an open source software layer called NVIDIA DSX OS for configuring, certifying, and maintaining accelerated Kubernetes infrastructure.
 NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) defines version-locked configuration recipes with pinned versions, dependency graphs, and health assertions, then renders them as bundles for deployment tools such as Argo CD, Flux, and Helm.
 NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine (NVCRE) validates workload readiness by running NCCL communication tests and training workloads with configurable performance thresholds, and bisects failing groups to identify suspect nodes.
 NVSentinel continuously monitors GPU, node, and network health signals, publishes node conditions, and when enabled can cordon, drain, and remediate faulty nodes before triggering revalidation with NVCRE.
 A lifecycle controller automates validation when nodes join the cluster or return after remediation, keeping them gated until tests pass, while AICR drift detection can trigger certification runs after infrastructure changes such as driver upgrades.
 Next Steps
 Read the NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) repository for installation instructions and examples.
 Read the NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine (NVCRE) repository for installation instructions and examples.
 Read the NVSentinel repository for installation instructions and examples.

 Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information.  Learn more 

 One underperforming GPU can slow an entire distributed training job. The node may pass basic health checks and show normal utilization, leaving operators to discover the problem only after the workload is running.

 These issues can appear at any point in a cluster’s lifecycle. A GPU cluster that passes readiness checks at handover changes as nodes are replaced, drivers are patched, and capacity is added. Without repeated validation, the original certification no longer reflects the cluster’s condition.

 This visibility gap wastes compute on failing nodes and leaves healthy nodes idle out of caution. Utilization metrics can mask these losses. Goodput, which is the volume of work successfully completed, provides a more useful measure of cluster efficiency. Maintaining cluster readiness requires validation throughout the cluster’s operational lifecycle—after configuration changes, as capacity grows, and before repaired nodes return to service.

 The NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together technologies for designing, building, and operating efficient, resilient AI factories. Its open source software layer, NVIDIA DSX OS, includes tools for configuring, certifying, and maintaining the health of accelerated Kubernetes infrastructure.

 Configure : NVIDIA AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) establishes a reproducible baseline for GPU-optimized Kubernetes infrastructure.

 Defines version-locked configuration recipes for components such as networking, storage, and drivers.

 Renders recipes as bundles for existing deployment tools.

 Certify : NVIDIA Cluster Readiness Engine (NVCRE) validates whether the cluster is ready to run production workloads.

 Tests GPUs, networking, and storage using AI workloads and diagnostics.

 Records certification results and helps identify faulty nodes.

 Operate : NVSentinel monitors cluster health and supports fault remediation and revalidation.

 Publishes node conditions based on GPU, node, and network health.

 When configured, cordons or taints unhealthy nodes, drains workloads, and remediates faults.

 Can trigger revalidation with NVCRE before nodes return to service.

 All three are open source projects licensed under Apache 2.0 and welcome external contributions.

 Before you begin, install and configure AICR , NVCRE , and NVSentinel using their installation guides. The examples assume access to a Kubernetes GPU cluster with the required CLIs, controllers, dependencies, and NVCRE test provider configured.

 This walkthrough follows one cluster through its lifecycle: configuration from a recipe, certification before production use, monitoring during operation, and recertification after repair. Each command is a step in that sequence.

 Configure: A baseline you can reproduce 

 AICR defines the cluster’s software baseline in version-controlled files and renders them into artifacts your existing deployment tooling applies. It generates and validates; your deployer applies and reconciles them. Declarative templates help detect configuration drift from manual changes and keep node configurations consistent after repairs.

 You describe the target environment. AICR resolves it against a library of validated overlays and emits a recipe:

aicr recipe --service eks --accelerator h100 --os ubuntu \
 --intent inference --platform dynamo -o recipe.yaml

 Each component entry in the resulting recipe pins a version and declares which dependencies must be healthy before the component is installed:

apiVersion: aicr.run/v1alpha2
componentRefs:
 - name: dynamo-platform
 chart: dynamo-platform
 namespace: dynamo-system
 source: https://helm.ngc.nvidia.com/nvidia/ai-dynamo
 type: Helm
 version: 1.4.2
 valuesFile: components/dynamo-platform/values.yaml
 dependencyRefs:
 - grove
 - cert-manager
 - kube-prometheus-stack
 - gpu-operator
 - kai-scheduler

 The recipe includes three key properties:

 Pinned versions: The version is fixed, helping you reproduce the software configuration and investigate failures. In contrast, a floating tag can point to a different software version over time, making failures harder to reproduce.

 A dependency graph: dependencyRefs declares what must be installed and healthy first. AICR resolves the graph when it renders the bundle, so the ordering is already encoded in the artifacts your deployer applies. You don’t need to specify that cert-manager comes before NVSentinel, and adding a component later doesn’t require renumbering.

 Health assertions per component: Each entry carries a healthCheckAsserts block that runs after installation and checks whether the component meets its configured health criteria. Kubernetes can report a pod stuck in CrashLoopBackOff as Running , so a check based only on the pod phase can miss a broken component. The shipped assertions filter on the container waiting reason rather than the pod phase alone.

 Rendering the recipe is a separate step that connects AICR to your existing pipeline:

aicr bundle --recipe recipe.yaml --deployer argocd --output ./bundles

 --deployer accepts helm , argocd , argocd-helm , flux , or helmfile , so the same validated recipe becomes Argo CD Application manifests, Flux resources, a Helmfile release graph, or plain Helm commands. You can keep your existing deployment tooling and use AICR to generate its configuration artifacts.

 Because the recipe is a file, you can use version history, code review, and drift detection to manage the baseline.

# Check a live cluster against the recipe's constraints
aicr validate --recipe recipe.yaml

# Compare a golden baseline against the live cluster, non-zero exit on drift
aicr diff --baseline ./golden.yaml --target cm://default/aicr-snapshot --fail-on-drift

 --fail-on-drift turns the drift check into a continuous integration (CI) gate rather than a report.

 Certify: Prove the cluster will run the job 

 The cluster is now built to a known baseline. It still needs workload validation. Standard health checks confirm that basic services are running. They don’t confirm that the cluster can run a demanding multinode job across its interconnect without stalling. NVCRE validates workload readiness by running training jobs and NVIDIA Collective Communication Library (NCCL) tests.

 NVSentinel manages validation requests, scheduling gates, quarantine, and repair, while NVCRE runs tests and records results. Table 1 shows how these responsibilities fit into the node validation lifecycle.

 Step Responsible component Action Outcome 
 1. Request and gate NVSentinel lifecycle manager; operators for upgrades or fabric changes Create a ValidationRequest for new or repaired nodes. After upgrades or fabric changes, operators cordon the nodes and create the request. A cordon or taint blocks scheduling on the nodes during validation. 
 2. Test and attribute NVCRE through nvcre-provider Run workloads and diagnostic tests. Bisect failing groups to identify suspect nodes. Test results identify suspect nodes. NVCRE doesn’t change the node state. 
 3. Record and evaluate NVCRE and NVSentinel lifecycle manager NVCRE records pass/fail results, failing node IDs, and failure reasons in the Certification resource. The lifecycle manager evaluates the results. The validation outcome determines whether the scheduling gate can be removed. 
 4. Resolve the gate NVSentinel lifecycle manager Remove or retain the scheduling gate based on validation results and any remaining tests. Pass: remove the configured gate once no other tests hold the node. Failure after retries: keep the node cordoned. 
 Table 1. Node validation duties, actions, and outcomes 

 A certification identifies the nodes to test, the categories to run, and the thresholds that determine whether the tests pass or fail:

apiVersion: nvcre.nvidia.com/v1alpha1
kind: Certification
metadata:
 name: gpu-cluster-cert
spec:
 target:
 nodeSelector:
 nvidia.com/gpu.present: "true"
 categories:
 - domain: communication
 variant: nccl-all-reduce
 - domain: training
 variant: nemotron5-8b
 options:
 thresholds:
 busBandwidthGBps: "value >= 300"

nvcrectl certification run --cert-file certification.yaml --wait
nvcrectl certification report gpu-cluster-cert -n <namespace>

 The report shows each category’s status, runtime, measured bandwidth, and the re

items.content:
Data Center / Cloud 

 Five Ways NVIDIA Co-Design Maximizes the Value of Every Byte in the AI Factory

 Nov 05, 2026

 By Eduardo Alvarez , Jamie Li and Ronil Prasad 

 Like

 Discuss (0)

 L 

 T 

 F 

 R 

 E 

 AI-Generated Summary

 NVFP4 reduces model footprint by approximately 3.5x versus FP16 and 1.8x versus FP8 while preserving accuracy, freeing HBM for KV cache, larger batches, and higher concurrency.
 Wide expert parallelism in TensorRT-LLM spreads experts across eight or more GPUs, leaving more HBM per GPU for cache and raising arithmetic intensity through weight reuse.
 NVIDIA Dynamo treats KV cache as a fleet-wide resource with KV-aware routing, disaggregated serving, and the KV Cache Runner that tiers blocks across GPU, CPU, and storage via NIXL.
 The NVIDIA Vera CPU provides 88 Olympus cores with 1.8x faster single-threaded performance and up to 1.5 TB of LPDDR5X connected coherently to Rubin at 1.8 TB/s over NVLink-C2C, staging idle KV cache during tool calls.
 NVIDIA CMX adds a pod-level G3.5 storage tier built on BlueField-4 STX, Spectrum-X, DOCA Memos, and Dynamo integration to share and reuse KV cache across nodes.
 Together these five co-designed levers enable Vera Rubin NVL72 to deliver up to 30x the throughput per megawatt of GB300 NVL72 from the same 288 GB per GPU.
 Next Steps
 Read the Inside NVIDIA Rubin GPU Architecture: Powering the Era of Agentic AI blog post for deeper architectural details.
 Explore the Optimizing Inference for Long Context and Large Batch Sizes with NVFP4 KV Cache blog post to learn KV cache optimization techniques.
 Review the Scaling Large MoE Models with Wide Expert Parallelism on NVL72 Rack Scale Systems blog post for expert parallelism implementation guidance.

 In an AI factory, high bandwidth memory (HBM)is the fastest, most expensive, and most contested memory tier. Every byte spent on a redundant weight copy, an idle session’s KV cache, or a recomputed prefix is a byte that is not being used to produce tokens. The question is no longer how much memory a GPU has, but how much useful work each byte delivers.

 The generational data in Figure 1 below shows why. From GB300 to NVIDIA Rubin, capacity held at 288 GB while bandwidth rose to 19.2 TB/s. 

 agentic throughput per megawatt grew far faster. On SemiAnalysis AgentX , which replays recorded coding-agent sessions with real tool-call gaps and growing context, NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 then delivers up to 30x the throughput per megawatt of GB300 NVL72 at 160 tokens per second per user.

 Figure 1. GPU throughput grew by 30x while HBM capacity remained approximately the same from GB300 NVL72 to Vera Rubin NVL72. 

 Capacity alone cannot explain a 30x gain delivered from the same 288 GB per GPU. The difference is how much useful work each byte delivers.

 NVIDIA treats this as a co-design problem that spans GPU architecture, the scale-up interconnect, serving software, the CPU, and storage. This post examines five ways that co-design maximizes the value of each byte of memory, from the bits that encode a single weight to the shared storage that preserves and reuses context across agentic turns and nodes.

 1. How does NVFP4 store more intelligence in fewer bytes? 

 The most direct way to raise the value of a byte is to make each value smaller without losing what it encodes. NVFP4 does this with a 4-bit E2M1 element and two levels of scaling: Every 16-value micro-block shares an FP8 (E4M3) scale factor, and a per-tensor FP32 scale sits on top. The result is a format that is small enough to free significant HBM, yet granular enough to preserve accuracy where naive 4-bit formats fall short.

 Figure 2. NVFP4 combines 4-bit values with block-level and tensor-level scaling. 

 Applied to weights, NVFP4 reduces the model footprint by approximately 3.5x relative to FP16 and 1.8x relative to FP8, freeing memory for what agentic inference needs most: more KV-cache capacity, larger batches, and higher concurrency. NVFP4 has become the default precision for open agentic benchmarks with strict accuracy requirements, including AA-AgentPerf, SemiAnalysis AgentX, and MLPerf Endpoints. Across these benchmarks and leading mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures, it delivers up to 4x the throughput of an FP8 baseline at the same interactivity (Figure 3 below). 

 Figure 3. NVFP4 delivers 4x the throughput per megawatt of FP8 at the same interactivity for DeepSeek R1 on GB300. 

 The same principle extends to the KV cache itself. NVFP4 KV cache cuts the cache footprint by up to 50% compared with FP8, so approximately 2x more context stays resident on device. Fewer evictions mean higher cache-hit rates during prefill, while a smaller cache means less bandwidth consumed during decode.

 NVFP4 shrinks the bytes. The next question is where those bytes live, and how many copies of them the AI factory has to keep.

 2. How does the NVLink scale-up domain turn 72 GPUs into one memory pool? 

 MoE models activate only a subset of parameters per token, but every expert’s weights must still live somewhere in HBM. When experts are packed onto a small number of GPUs, each GPU spends a large share of its memory on weights, and each decode step pays a heavy weight-loading cost for the MoE GroupGEMMs. The bytes are resident, but they are not working hard.

 Wide expert parallelism (Wide-EP) in NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM changes that ratio by spreading experts across eight or more GPUs. With DeepSeek-R1 at EP64, each GPU holds four experts per layer, or 232 expert blocks across 58 MoE layers out of 14,848 in the full model. Fewer expert weights per GPU means:

 Capacity: More HBM per GPU is left for KV cache, larger batches, and higher concurrency.

 Arithmetic intensity: GroupGEMM kernels reuse each loaded weight across more tokens, raising FLOPs per byte.

 Balance: The Expert Parallel Load Balancer (EPLB) redistributes hot and cold experts between forward passes, so no GPU’s memory is overcommitted while another sits idle.

 Figure 5. GB300 NVL72 delivers 10x the token throughput per megawatt of H200 NVL8 at 100 tokens per second per user. 

 This only works because the scale-up domain makes remote bytes nearly as useful as local ones. Every MoE layer triggers all-to-all dispatch and combine traffic, and without a high-bandwidth fabric, those collectives would erase the gains. On GB200 NVL72, 130 TB/s of aggregate NVLink bandwidth absorbs that traffic, and large EP (EP32) delivers up to 1.8x more output tokens per second per GPU than small EP (EP8) at 100 tokens per second per user.

 Vera Rubin NVL72 extends the same design point. Each Rubin GPU brings up to 288 GB of HBM4 and 3.0 TB/s of NVLink 6 bandwidth, for roughly 20.7 TB of HBM4 across the rack. Rubin also adds inline memory tensor acceleratory (TMA) descriptor updates, so one shared descriptor can serve every expert with a common layout, reducing the metadata overhead that grows with expert count.

 Wide-EP decides where weight bytes live. The next lever decides whether KV cache bytes, once computed, are ever computed again.

 3. How does NVIDIA Dynamo make every cached byte count? 

 The key-value (KV) cache stores intermediate attention calculations from previously processed tokens so the model can reuse them instead of recomputing them. This inference state is ephemeral and can be evicted and recomputed when needed, but KV cache is only valuable if it is reused. Agentic workloads are full of reuse opportunities: system prompts, tool schemas, shared documents, and the growing history of a multistep task. But if a request lands on a GPU that does not hold its prefix, or if that prefix was evicted moments earlier, the system pays for prefill again. The bytes existed; they were just in the wrong place.

 NVIDIA Dynamo is the distributed serving layer that closes this gap. It treats KV cache as a fleet-wide resource rather than a per-GPU side effect, and it does so through three co-designed capabilities:

 KV-aware routing: The Dynamo router tracks where KV blocks reside and considers both cached-prefix overlap and worker load when placing requests. It balances existing context against the cost of sending work to an utilized GPU and turns potential recomputations into cache hits. 

 Disaggregated serving: Prefill and decode run on separate GPU pools, each sized for its own compute and memory profile. Decode GPUs can dedicate HBM to KV cache and batch size rather than reserving headroom for bursty prefill.

 KV Cache Runner (KVCR): This tracks where every block lives across configured GPU, pinned CPU, and storage tiers, including local SSDs and mounted network filesystems. A prefix preserved outside HBM can be restored when a later request needs it, allowing useful context to survive GPU eviction and continue saving prefill work. KVCR uses the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) for its storage-transfer paths, allowing cached blocks to move while the GPU processes other work. KVCR also enables distributed reuse, with router-provided hints helping a selected worker retrieve cached context from a peer, while the inference engine retains control of GPU memory and local host offloading. The additional KVCR-Guard feature preserves committed KVCR-managed host-memory cache across an engine failure as long as the guard service and host remain available.
